Most US employers must keep a log of work-related injuries and illnesses and, at the end of each
year, post a summary on **OSHA Form 300A**: the number of deaths, cases with days away from work,
cases with job transfer or restriction, and other recordable cases, plus the number of employees
and hours worked. Since 2016, larger establishments (250 or more employees) and establishments
with 20 to 249 employees in designated high-hazard industries must submit their 300A to OSHA's
Injury Tracking Application (ITA). OSHA publishes every submission, with the employer's name. This
notebook uses calendar years 2016 to 2025. Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

There is one establishment file per year (about 15 MB each). `read_year()` loads one; the summary
table has totals for every year.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules"
read_module <- function(module, folder, name) {
  local <- file.path("..", "..", module, "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, module, "data", folder, name),
           show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 100000) |>
    # Identifiers are codes, not numbers (ZIP codes and EINs can start with 0)
    mutate(across(any_of(c("establishment_id", "naics_code")), as.character),
           across(any_of("zip_code"), \(x) str_pad(x, 5, pad = "0")),
           across(any_of("ein"), \(x) str_pad(x, 9, pad = "0")))
}
read_year <- function(year) {
  read_module("us-osha-ita-summary", "tidy", sprintf("establishments_%d.csv.gz", year))
}

summary_tbl <- read_module("us-osha-ita-summary", "tidy", "summary_by_industry.csv.gz")
est24 <- read_year(2024)

# Rates per 100 full-time workers (200,000 hours): total recordable cases (TCR) and cases with
# days away, restriction or transfer (DART)
add_rates <- function(d) {
  mutate(d, tcr = total_cases / total_hours_worked * 200000,
            dart = (dafw_cases + djtr_cases) / total_hours_worked * 200000)
}
```

# Part 1. Who reports?

```{r who}
summary_tbl |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(establishments = sum(establishments),
            employees_millions = sum(annual_average_employees[plausible]) / 1e6)

est24 |>
  count(size, ownership) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ownership, values_from = n)

est24 |>
  count(naics_sector, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8)

# Share of establishments that reported no injuries or illnesses at all
est24 |>
  group_by(size) |>
  summarise(establishments = n(), share_no_cases = round(mean(!any_cases, na.rm = TRUE), 2))
```

**Questions**

1. About how many establishments submit each year, and how many employees do they cover? The US
   has about 135 million private-sector employees. What share do these data cover?
2. Which industry sectors submit the most? Why might retail trade, manufacturing and health care
   dominate (hint: which establishments must submit)?
3. What share of establishments report no injuries or illnesses at all? Does that share differ by
   size? Why might it?

# Part 2. Injury rates by industry

These rates use only records flagged `plausible` (see the data dictionary).

```{r industry}
summary_tbl |>
  filter(year == 2024, plausible) |>
  group_by(naics_sector) |>
  summarise(across(c(establishments, total_hours_worked, total_cases, dafw_cases, djtr_cases), sum)) |>
  add_rates() |>
  filter(establishments >= 500) |>
  mutate(across(c(tcr, dart), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  arrange(desc(tcr)) |>
  select(naics_sector, establishments, tcr, dart)
```

**Questions**

1. Which sectors have the highest total recordable case rates? Which have the lowest?
2. The BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII module) reports a TCR of about 2.4
   for all private industry in 2024. Why is the ITA rate for most sectors higher? (Think about
   which establishments must submit.)
3. What is the difference between the TCR and the DART rate? Why might an employer prefer to
   restrict a worker's duties rather than send them home?
4. Construction and mining have low rates here, although both are hazardous industries. Why
   might that be? (Hint: what is an "establishment" for a construction company?)

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Establishments differ

```{r establishments}
warehouses <- est24 |>
  filter(plausible, str_starts(naics_code, "4931"), annual_average_employees >= 100) |>
  add_rates()

nrow(warehouses)
summary(warehouses$tcr)

ggplot(warehouses, aes(tcr)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 30)) +
  labs(title = "Warehouses with 100+ employees, 2024",
       x = "Total recordable cases per 100 full-time workers", y = "Establishments")

# Companies with many warehouses
warehouses |>
  filter(!is.na(company_name)) |>
  group_by(company_name) |>
  summarise(warehouses = n(), employees = sum(annual_average_employees),
            tcr = sum(total_cases) / sum(total_hours_worked) * 200000,
            dart = sum(dafw_cases + djtr_cases) / sum(total_hours_worked) * 200000) |>
  filter(warehouses >= 20) |>
  mutate(across(c(tcr, dart), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  arrange(desc(employees)) |>
  head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. Describe the distribution of injury rates among large warehouses. What is the median? How
   high do the highest go?
2. Compare the companies with many warehouses. Which have the highest rates? Company names are
   entered by the employer, so the same company may appear under several names. How would you
   check?
3. A company with a low reported rate may be safer, or may record fewer injuries. What other
   information would help you tell the difference?

# Part 4. Trends, and COVID-19

```{r trends}
trend <- summary_tbl |>
  filter(plausible) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(across(c(total_hours_worked, total_cases, dafw_cases, djtr_cases, injuries,
                     respiratory_conditions), sum)) |>
  add_rates() |>
  mutate(respiratory_per_10k = respiratory_conditions / total_hours_worked * 2e7)

ggplot(trend, aes(year, tcr)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2016:2025) +
  labs(title = "Total recordable case rate, ITA establishments", x = NULL, y = "TCR")

summary_tbl |>
  filter(plausible, year %in% 2019:2023) |>
  group_by(year, naics_sector) |>
  summarise(respiratory = sum(respiratory_conditions), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(naics_sector) |>
  filter(sum(respiratory) > 5000) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = respiratory)
```

**Questions**

1. How did the overall rate change from 2016 to 2025? What happened in 2020 to 2022?
2. Which sector reported the most respiratory illnesses in 2020 and 2021? Why?
3. The set of establishments that submit changes from year to year. Why does that make the trend
   harder to interpret?

# Part 6. Data quality

```{r quality}
all_years <- bind_rows(lapply(2016:2025, read_year))

all_years |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(establishments = n(),
            share_implausible = round(mean(!plausible), 3),
            zero_hours = sum(total_hours_worked == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            revised = sum(revised))

# Examples of implausible records
all_years |>
  filter(!plausible, annual_average_employees > 0) |>
  mutate(hours_per_employee = round(total_hours_worked / annual_average_employees)) |>
  select(year, establishment_name, annual_average_employees, total_hours_worked,
         hours_per_employee) |>
  slice_sample(n = 8)

# How much does the flag matter?
all_years |>
  filter(year == 2024, total_hours_worked > 0) |>
  group_by(plausible) |>
  summarise(establishments = n(), employees = sum(annual_average_employees),
            tcr = sum(total_cases, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_hours_worked) * 200000)
```

**Questions**

1. What kinds of errors do the implausible records show? Suggest how some of them happened.
2. The flag uses 250 to 8,760 hours per employee. Is that a sensible range? What happens to the
   overall rate if you include the implausible records?
3. Describe one more check you would add, and code it.

# Part 7. Following establishments over time

The `establishment_id` stays the same from year to year, so we can follow establishments.

```{r panel}
panel <- all_years |>
  filter(plausible, year %in% c(2022, 2023), annual_average_employees >= 100) |>
  add_rates() |>
  select(establishment_id, year, naics_sector, tcr) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = tcr, names_prefix = "tcr_") |>
  filter(!is.na(tcr_2022), !is.na(tcr_2023)) |>
  mutate(group_2022 = ntile(tcr_2022, 5))

nrow(panel)
panel |>
  group_by(group_2022) |>
  summarise(establishments = n(), mean_tcr_2022 = mean(tcr_2022), mean_tcr_2023 = mean(tcr_2023)) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("mean"), \(x) round(x, 2)))

cor(panel$tcr_2022, panel$tcr_2023)
```

**Questions**

1. Establishments in the highest fifth in 2022 had lower rates in 2023, and the lowest fifth had
   higher rates. Explain this pattern (regression to the mean).
2. OSHA might target inspections at establishments with the highest rates. If it inspects them
   and their rates fall the next year, can it conclude the inspections worked? How would you
   design a fair evaluation?
3. How strongly are an establishment's rates in consecutive years correlated? What does that
   suggest about using one year's rate to judge a workplace?

**Your answer:**



# Part 8. Linking to the case detail data

Since 2023, establishments with 100 or more employees in designated industries also submit their
Form 300 and 301 case details. The [ITA case detail module](../../us-osha-ita-case-detail/) has a
random sample of these cases, which link to the 300A records by `establishment_id` and year.

```{r linking}
cases <- read_module("us-osha-ita-case-detail", "sample", "ita_case_detail_sample.csv") |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year_of_filing))

incident_types <- c("1" = "Injury", "2" = "Skin disorder", "3" = "Respiratory condition",
                    "4" = "Poisoning", "5" = "Hearing loss", "6" = "Other illness")
linked <- cases |>
  mutate(type_of_incident = unname(incident_types[as.character(type_of_incident)])) |>
  select(establishment_id, year, type_of_incident, incident_outcome) |>
  inner_join(all_years |> filter(plausible) |> add_rates() |>
               select(establishment_id, year, naics_sector, dart),
             by = c("establishment_id", "year"))

nrow(cases)
nrow(linked)

# Do cases from high-rate establishments differ from those at low-rate ones?
linked |>
  mutate(dart_group = if_else(dart >= median(dart), "Higher DART", "Lower DART")) |>
  count(dart_group, type_of_incident) |>
  group_by(dart_group) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3)) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = dart_group, values_from = share)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of the sampled cases link to a plausible 300A record? Why do some drop out (hint:
   look at the filter in the join)? What could it mean for an analysis if those cases differ from
   the rest?
2. Compare the types of incident at establishments with higher and lower DART rates. Do the
   differences make sense?
3. Propose a research question that needs both the case details and the 300A hours worked. Which
   tables would you join, and what would you calculate?

**Your answer:**
